title: Ancient Pocket Change Reveals Special Status of Rome’s “Little Englanders” - Nautilus
gist: Coins excavated beneath Rome's Palazzo della Rovere — the site where Nero's theater was found in 2023 — provide the first material remains of the Schola Saxonum, medieval Rome's English quarter, as described by Cambridge's Francesca Tinti and Rory Naismith.

insights.claim: Archaeologists began excavating beneath the walled garden of Rome's Palazzo della Rovere in 2020 and by 2023 announced they had found the ruins of Emperor Nero's theater.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.locator: If you’ve ever lost some pocket change

themes.theme: First physical evidence of Rome's English quarter

insights.claim: Coins unearthed at the Palazzo della Rovere site tell a story about the Schola Saxonum, medieval Rome's 'Little England' English quarter.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Coin finds illuminate medieval monetary and pilgrimage networks.
insights.locator: If you’ve ever lost some pocket change

insights.claim: Francesca Tinti of the University of Cambridge said that before this discovery there were no material remains of the English quarter in Rome at all.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.quote: Before this big discovery, we never had any material remains of the English quarter in Rome

insights.claim: Tinti and Cambridge collaborator Rory Naismith detailed the coin find in a chapter of the book 'Rome and the Others (300-1000): Foreigners in the City Between Conflicts and Integration'.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: The coins suggest English pilgrims in medieval Rome held a special status, apparently not needing to secure travel money.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Insight into early medieval cross-border money flows and privileged foreign communities.
insights.quote: These pilgrims didn’t have to secure travel money
insights.locator: Ancient Pocket Change Reveals Special Status
